title: Optimized protocol for live-cell analysis of kinetochore fiber maturation in Indian muntjac cells
protocol: Set temperature of the objective controlled heating band to 37.5°C, 1 hour before imaging.
Place a temperature sensor on the imaging dish containing water or medium, just above the objective-acquisition spot overnight (approximately 16 hours).
Check the temperature in the morning; if not stable at 37°C, adjust the set-point accordingly and repeat the measurement.
Set CO2 levels to 5%, if the microscope is equipped with a source of CO2.
Incubate cells with 3 μM MG-132 (proteasome inhibitor) to induce metaphase arrest, together with 75 nM of the Halotag® fluorescent ligand JF646 ∼30 min prior to imaging.
Place the imaging chamber on the microscope.
Co-align the excitation and STED beams at the Abberior’s Inspector software.
Scan the coverslip for metaphase cells using the eye pieces.
Acquire a confocal image of the full spindle as a pre-recording example of spindle length to monitor phototoxicity and photobleaching.
Adjust 488 nm laser intensity (∼0.2 kW/cm² is enough to define the position of the kinetochore).
Adjust 640 nm excitation laser intensity (∼1.2–1.8 kW/cm²).
Adjust 775 nm depletion laser intensity to ∼27.5 MW/cm².
Define the radius of the bi-vortex phase mask (rho value).
Set time-lapse to 750 ms for data collection.
Collect 80 frames during data collection.
Define pixel size to 40 nm.
Define pinhole size to 0.8 airy unit.
Select a smaller ROI that includes both sister kinetochores and one k-fiber in the same focal plane for live-cell imaging.
Ensure typical ROI size used is ∼2.5 × 6.5 μm (width × length).
Selecting a ROI that includes the kinetochore pair ensures the kinetochore of interest is always in frame.
Ensure the full-length k-fiber is within a single focal plane.
Acquire the STED time lapse movie according to defined conditions.
Take a confocal image of the full spindle post-recording to monitor phototoxicity and photobleaching.
Save the .msr file.
Open the .msr file in Fiji (ImageJ) for data analysis.
Place the chamber on the microscope.
Align the microsurgery laser by obtaining a coarse prediction of the laser position by looking at breakage marks on the glass coverslip.
Focus the coverslip by going a few micrometers below the interphase cells.
Hit the glass with 1 pulse of laser to identify its position and mark the coordinates on the software.
Adjust laser power to the minimum required to break the glass for increased accuracy in position prediction.
Refine position prediction by identifying the center of the signal depletion region after surgery.
Focus on a bright fluorescent structure that is stationary.
Hit the structure with one/multiple pulses of laser to identify its position and adjust the coordinates on the software.
Adjust laser power to the minimum required to damage the structure.
Find a compromise between the minimum laser power and number of pulses required to cause damage.
Do small adjustments in the Z-position while applying pulses of laser to the sample to find the focal plane.
Scan the coverslip for metaphase cells.
After selecting a cell, focus a k-fiber where microsurgery will be performed.
Acquire a pre-surgery fluorescent image of the entire area of the cell.
Select a focal plane that contains the entire k-fiber where microsurgery will be performed.
Apply 2–5 sequential pulses (spaced by 0.35 μm) along the transverse axis of the fiber, combined with 3 pulses in Z (spaced by 0.4 μm) at each point.
Proceed with imaging immediately after performing the cut.
Proceed with imaging immediately after surgery.
Sample the entire cell area every 1 second for 2 minutes.
Sample the entire cell area every 1 minute up to 5 minutes.
Use both 488 nm and 567 nm excitation wavelengths on a single focal plane.
